widget.solution:
from fractions import Fraction


def option_book(strikes):
    """For each strike K, return (K, call, put, straddle,
    parity_ok) on the sum of two dice: exact Fractions, and
    parity_ok True when call - put == 7 - K."""
    sums = [a + b for a in range(1, 7) for b in range(1, 7)]
    out = []
    for k in strikes:
        c = Fraction(sum(max(s - k, 0) for s in sums), 36)
        p = Fraction(sum(max(k - s, 0) for s in sums), 36)
        out.append((k, c, p, c + p, c - p == 7 - k))
    return out

items.title: Checking a set of quotes
items.prose: An interviewer shows quotes on contracts tied to one die. They ask whether you can make money for sure.
items.question: Put the checks in order, and leave out the one that does not belong.

lines.text: Write every contract's payoff on each face.
Find a combination to test, such as one whose payoffs cancel on every face.
Price it at the quotes: buy at asks, sell at bids. Is it in profit on every face?
Check the sizes shown at each price, and trade the smallest.
Trade the biggest-looking gap first, then check the payoffs.
lines.why: Trading before checking can leave a leg open. A gap is only an arbitrage once no face can lose.

items.title: Mock round, part 1: play
items.prose: The mock round. You make the market in the 7-call on two dice, size 1 or 2, width 0.2 to 0.4, limit 4. Skew 0.05 per call held. The interviewer is listed as `scripted`; the first die turns before turn 3.
items.question: Finish the five turns with a P&L of at least £0.80 and no rule breaks.

schedule.text: A market in the 7-call on the sum of two dice: it pays $(S - 7)^+$. Fair is $35/36 = 0.97$.
The first die shows 2. The call now pays only if the second die is 6: fair $1/6 = 0.17$.

items.title: Mock round, part 2: say it
items.prompt:
Narrate the mock round aloud, timed: about ten minutes, kept with a watch. Use the model run. Sell 2 calls at 1.1, then buy 2 back at 0.2 after the first die shows 2.

On turn 2 the interviewer adds a parity break. The 7-put is 0.7 to 0.8 and the sum 6.9 to 7.1. Say what trade it allows and what it locks.

Say every fair value with its arithmetic, and the ledger after each trade. Give the worst outcome for your position and the final P&L. Then write it out and mark it.
items.model:
**Before the first quote.** "The 7-call pays the sum less 7 when the sum is above 7. Sums 8 to 12 pay 1 to 5 on 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 rolls. That is 35 over 36, so fair is 0.97. I quote 0.9 at 1.1 for 2, width 0.2."

**Turn 1: they buy 2 at 1.1.** "Short 2 calls at 1.1, cash £2.20. At fair 0.97 I am up 2 × 0.13 = £0.26. Short calls lose on high sums: the worst is 12, where I owe 2 × 5 = 10, a loss of £7.80. I skew up 0.1 for the short 2: 1.0 at 1.2."

**Turn 2: the parity offer.** The interviewer also quotes the 7-put at 0.7 to 0.8 and the sum at 6.9 to 7.1. "Parity says call − put = 7 − 7 = 0. A put at 0.8 plus a sum at 7.1, less the 7 they pay together, is a call for 0.9. I sold calls at 1.1, so buying that for 0.9 locks 0.20 a set. On my 2 that is £0.40, whatever the dice. This game trades only the call, so I note it and carry on."

**The first die shows 2.** "Now the call pays only if the second die is 6, and then 1: fair 1/6 = 0.17. Short 2 at 1.1, I am up 2 × (1.1 − 0.17) = £1.87. Centre 0.17 + 0.1 = 0.27, call it 0.3: 0.2 at 0.4."

**Turn 4: they sell 2 at 0.2.** "I buy back 2 at 0.2. Flat now, with cash 2.20 − 0.40 = £1.80 locked. Centre 0.17: 0.1 at 0.3."

**Settlement.** The second die is 3, the sum 5, so the call pays 0. "Flat, so the P&L is the cash: +£1.80. Had I stayed short and the second die been 6, I would have owed 2 × 1 = 2."

**Review.** "The edge came from updating. I sold at 1.1 a call worth 0.97, and bought it back at 0.2 for 0.17. The parity gap was worth 0.20 a set. Every number had its reason, and I said the worst case before it could happen."

rubric.text: Fair values with arithmetic: 35/36 before the die, 1/6 after the 2.
Finds the parity trade: put at 0.8 and sum at 7.1 against the call at 1.1, for 0.20 a set.
States the ledger after each trade: short 2, cash £2.20; then flat, cash £1.80.
Names the worst case for the short calls: a sum of 12 owes 10, a loss of £7.80.
Moves the quote after the die and after each trade, with the skew.
States the final P&L, +£1.80, and reviews where the edge came from.
